subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-49, to provide for the establishment of a national energy board.
He said: In the discussion on the resolution prior to the introduction of Bill C-49, all who spoke appeared to be agreed upon the fundamental purpose of the measure, which is to establish a national energy board with a view to assuring to the people of Canada the best use of the energy resources of this country. Now that hon. members have the bill before them and as the discussion develops, I hope they will agree that the principles underlying the bill and the means by which we seek to apply those principles are also generally acceptable. Although the bill comprises 101 sections, it is very largely based on the relevant sections of the Pipe Lines Act and on the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act. What is new is important but not extensive.
It is now my intention to explain the main functions of the board as set forth in the bill and as contemplated by the government; to compare some aspects of the bill with relevant recommendations in the first report of the royal commission on energy, and to draw the attention of the house to certain limitations upon the powers of the board.
I would first point out that the bill will provide simpler machinery for dealing with matters relating to oil and gas and the pipe lines to transport them than has existed in the past, and also simpler than that contemplated by the royal commission on energy. In the past the board of transport commissioners has had certain responsibilities in respect of the construction and operation of pipe lines as set forth in the Pipe Lines Act, while the Minister of Trade and Commerce has had certain responsibilities under the Exportation of Power and Fluids and the Importation of Gas Act.
Procedures under the two acts have been separate and not entirely parallel. In the case of gas exports involving pipe line construction, applicants have had to satisfy two different agencies. The effect of the Borden commission's recommendation would have been to require applicants seeking permission to build pipe lines coming under the jurisdiction of parliament to satisfy two different

bodies, the national energy board and the board of transport commissioners. The bill now before you will replace the Pipe Lines Act and the Exportation of Power and Fluids and the Importation of Gas Act. It will concentrate within the single agency of the national energy board the functions formerly carried out by the board of transport commissioners and those carried out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in respect to import and export licences for gas and export licences for electrical power. As in the case of the Pipe Lines Act, certain sections of the Railway Act will be incorporated in this bill by reference.
So much jurisprudence has grown up concerning these sections and so many rights have been created through their application that it would have been a most complex and time-consuming task, delaying the presentation of this legislation, to restate them afresh with any confidence that the results would be satisfactory and that existing rights would be protected. Notwithstanding this qualification, I suggest that this bill should commend itself to the house on the ground that it will simplify what has been a complicated and confusing statutory situation and streamline the procedures which must be followed by companies wishing to construct pipe lines.
Turning now to the functions which the bill will establish for the national energy board, I would first direct attention to the board's advisory responsibilities. They are the functions by which the board will be kept informed of changing circumstances and requirements and will thus be enabled to give expert advice to the government. The need for a central body charged with responsibility for research and comparative study of the various forms and sources of energy has long been apparent. Some useful work has been done in the past, both by ad hoc bodies such as the Gordon commission and the Borden commission and, in various special fields, on a more continuing basis by various departments and agencies. However, most energy sources are to some degree and in some circumstances interchangeable, and in some fuel applications there is intense competition.
The balance between the various energy sources has changed very markedly over recent years, and we may expect it will continue to change in the future. Such changes have important implications for national policy, and it is therefore highly desirable that a continuing and consistent study of energy matters be carried forward by a competent body.
In framing the advisory functions of the board we have had in mind, among other
National Energy Board things, certain recommendations of the Borden commission, in particular recommendation 20. Since the language of that recommendation appeared open to the interpretation of requiring intrusion upon matters which are under the jurisdiction of the provinces, it is made clear that the responsibilities of the board for making continuing studies and for making recommendations to the minister are to be limited to those matters over which parliament has jurisdiction.
Also, whereas the intent of recommendation 20(b) was apparently that the national energy board should assist other agencies-and this is of course a laudable objective-it was considered by the government to be undesirable to allow the board on its own initiative to proffer advice and recommendations to any minister or any federal agency, since the indiscriminate use of such authority could give rise to confusion and uncertainty in the formulation of government policy. The bill therefore requires that requests for assistance from the board be channelled through the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Under the advisory functions provision has been made in general terms for arrangements such as those specified in recommendation 29 of the Borden commission:
That, if possible, reciprocal arrangements be made with the United States of America for a commissioner of the federal power commission of that country to sit as an ad hoc observer, but without vote, when the national energy board is considering any application for a licence for the export of natural gas from Canada to the United States or for the import of natural gas into Canada; and for a member of the national energy board to sit as an ad hoc observer, but without vote, when the federal power commission is considering the correlative application for the licence to import from or export to Canada such natural gas.
The objective which the Borden commission appears to have had in mind was the desirable one of establishing liaison with the federal power commission in order to avoid the misunderstandings and deadlocks which might all too easily arise in the matter of the export and import of natural gas. We desire that a basis of effective co-operation in satisfying our respective national interests be established with the federal power commission, but the arrangements suggested by the Borden commission raise questions for both countries which may have implications not fully foreseen by the commission. Both the federal power act and the natural gas act might have to be amended by congress to enable the federal power commission to participate in such arrangements.
The federal power commission is, we understand, required to conduct its deliberations, as contrasted with its hearings, in private without any interested party being present.
3924	HOUSE OF
National Energy Board From another viewpoint, it would be embarrassing for either government to have the regulatory agency of the other government make a decision adverse to its interests when a member of its own regulatory body had participated in the events leading up to such a decision. For these reasons the bill will give the board a general power to recommend the establishment of co-operative relationships with other agencies. Under this power a satisfactory relationship will, we are sure, be worked out and be given appropriate recognition by such action of the two parent governments as may be necessary. The best solution will have to be found in the light of experience and the possibilities that exist for such co-operation.
Perhaps this would be an appropriate point to mention that the government has not accepted the Borden commission's recommendation 28, "that a member of the national energy board be appointed in due time to the Canadian section of the international joint commission." The recommendation appears to be inconsistent with the principle that a quasi-judicial body such as the latter should not have as a member representative of a party which may be directly interested in proceedings before it. Presumably such a member would be expected to disqualify himself in international joint commission cases in which the national energy board had such an interest, a step which would make the dual membership arrangement sterile.
To revert to the research and advisory functions of the board as set forth in the bill, hon. members will have noted that the board will be expected to avoid unnecessary duplication of existing research facilities and sources of information within the government of Canada. Conversely, where such information is not readily available from these or other sources of information, the board will be enabled to secure any information it needs by exercising the powers of commissioners under part I of the Inquiries Act. The relevant paragraph of the Inquiries Act is section 4, which reads:
The commissioners have the power of summoning before them any witnesses, and of requiring them to give evidence on oath, or on solemn affirmation if they are persons entitled to affirm in civil matters, and orally or in writing, and to produce such documents and things as the commissioners deem requisite to the full investigation of the matters into which they are appointed to examine.
This power should, in the view of the government, be given the board to enable it to fill certain gaps in the information available to it through other channels. For instance, section 15 of the Statistics Act prohibits the release by the dominion bureau of statistics of figures relating to individual companies, with the exception of carriers and public


utilities. It will be recalled that the Borden commission in support of its recommendation 19, that the importation into Canada of crude oil and petroleum products be made subject to licence granted by the national energy board, argued that such licensing was required-
-to provide the government of Canada, through the national energy board, with basic information respecting the origins, cost, transportation charges and laid-down cost in Canada of crude oil and petroleum products-
Licensing appears to be an inappropriate method for obtaining the desired information. The preferable method of ensuring that necessary information can be obtained is through the powers conferred by the Inquiries Act. The exercise of these powers is restricted to the advisory functions of the board.
The next broad function of the board would be the exercise of control over the construction and operation of pipe lines for the transmission of hydrocarbons and the issuance of certificates of convenience and necessity to authorize the construction and operation of such pipe lines. This part of the bill is drawn very substantially from the present Pipe Lines Act. The national energy board would, however, replace the board of transport commissioners as the responsible agency.
It is here that one of the important differences exists between this bill and the recommendations of the Borden report. Recommendation 15 of that report was, in essence, that anyone wishing to build an oil or gas pipe line subject to the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada must obtain a certificate from the national energy board; recommendation 32 was that no application for leave to construct a pipe line should be entertained by the board of transport commissioners unless the applicant had such a certificate from the national energy board. The board of transport commissioners would also regulate oil and gas pipe line transmission rates.
The Borden commission did not believe that any purpose would be served by transferring these functions to the national energy board. Transfer of the board of transport commissioners' functions would, in the view of the commission, not only mean an unjustified duplication of administrative machinery and personnel but would ignore the whole of the experience in this type of work now embodied in the board of transport commissioners. In the commission's opinion, as expressed in the report-
-the problem involved in assessing Canada's energy resources and needs and in relating these and the implications of other energy studies-

Which the commission has recommended should be carried out by the national energy board:
*-to the issuance or withholding of licences or certificates of public convenience are distinct from the regulatory function which the commission has recommended should be carried out by the board of transport commissioners with respect to oil and gas pipe line companies.
In practice any duplication of administrative machinery and personnel would be more apparent than real. The personnel of the board of transport commissioners and its staff who are familiar with the oil and gas industry are not as numerous as the commission may have thought. The board of transport commissioners has had one engineer employed full time on pipe line work, one engineer part time and one stenographer. Changes have recently occurred in the board itself due to resignations and retirements. Consequently in transferring these functions to the energy board there would seem to be little danger either of duplicating personnel or of losing valuable experience.
On the other hand, to ask two boards to deal with somewhat different but closely related aspects of pipe line matters would certainly invite duplication and confusion, both within the government service and among applicants who would have to appear before both boards, and who would find difficulty in satisfying either board in the absence of decision by the other. We do not wish to add to the administrative burden on industry in submitting applications.
Under the present bill, therefore, the board of transport commissioners will have no power over pipe lines, except in so far as its permission is required for the crossing of railways by pipe lines. The energy board will issue certificates of public convenience and necessity which at the same time will be "leave to construct" orders, in the sense in which that term has been used by the board of transport commissioners. The energy board will also issue "leave to open" orders. That is, it will discharge the functions now held by the board of transport commissioners as regards the public safety aspect of pipe line regulations. It will also regulate the transmission charges of both oil and gas pipe lines, a function in which the board of transport commissioners has had no experience but which the Borden commission recommended it should assume.
Although it was not so recommended by the Borden commission, all certificates issued by the energy board will be subject to the approval of the governor in council, as will any regulations made by the board governing their issuance. New major pipe line projects appear likely to raise questions of national
National Energy Board policy so important that decision on them should be reviewed in this way.
It will be noted that certificates are to be issued only for pipe lines transmitting hydrocarbons. The by-products of the processing of gas, mentioned in recommendation 15 of the Borden report, will consequently remain unregulated as regards transmission by pipe lines unless they fall within the definition of hydrocarbons. Sulphur, the chief by-product, which is not a hydrocarbon, is neither a form nor a source of energy, and consequently lies outside the area of reference of this legislation.
In addition to certificates of public convenience and necessity, the Borden commission suggested that licences also be required. Recommendation 16 reads as follows:
That the national energy board be authorized to require any company engaged in the transmission across provincial boundaries by pipe line of crude oil and petroleum products and natural gas and byproducts thereof, to obtain a licence from such board.
Recommendation 20(f)(ii) suggested that the board should have authority to grant, revoke or suspend such licences, upon such terms and subject to such conditions, if any, that the board might decide. Recommendation 21(c) suggested that among the factors to be considered in issuing such licences should be: (i) the direction of movement and destination of the contents of the pipe line; and, (ii) the volume proposed to be transmitted. The licensing of interprovincial oil or gas movements was included since, in the commission's view, and again I quote the commission's words-
"*-control of such matters as the volume so transmitted. the direction of flow and the destination of the oil and gas within Canada is essential to ensure that the public interest can be protected in the effective use of these resources".
Licensing would not be on an annual basis, but the original licence would be re-examined whenever changes in the operation of a line were to be made with regard to direction of flow or substantial increases in volume.
None of these recommendations has been implemented in this bill. The view has been taken that the direction of movement, as well as the initial and ultimate capacity of any such pipe line, would have been specified in the application for a certificate of public convenience and necessity. Any change of direction, or capacity beyond the specified limits, would require application for a further certificate, so for these reasons a licence would be superfluous.
An extension of a pipe line would also require an application for an additional certificate. A change in the proportion of throughput delivered to various destinations along
3926	HOUSE OF
National Energy Board the certificated route would in most circumstances result from normal business considerations, and would hardly require a licence for any reason of public policy. There is intense competition among the various fuels and energy sources; therefore there is a strong impetus for a pipe line company to maximize its volume and minimize its unit costs in all markets in which it can compete.
Service to new markets by construction of new sales laterals would involve either (1) construction of laterals contemplated in the original application and therefore covered by the original certificate; (2) construction of long new laterals not contemplated in the original application and therefore requiring a new certificate; (3) construction of short laterals coming within an exemption procedure provided in the bill; or, (4) extension of service by direction of the board, also as provided in the bill. None of these cases would appear to require a licence, as distinct from the required certificate.
Finally, the volume to be transmitted would either be within the capacity originally certificated, within which range business conditions and decisions would appear to be the effective determinants, rather than the licensing procedure; or major increases in volume would require major looping, which would require a further certificate.
There is an historical justification for export licences, in that electricity and gas exports have been dealt with under earlier legislation in order to ensure that these energy forms are not alienated unless they are clearly surplus to present and foreseeable Canadian requirements. An export licence is also required to satisfy the requirements of the federal power commission as to the availability of gas to fill export contracts. However, the considerations affecting the public interest in the operation of pipe lines within Canada are different; non-discrimination, non-exploitation of quasi-monopoly positions, avoidance of unnecessary and uneconomic duplication of facilities, economic access to energy resources, and the public safety are the kinds of consideration that underlie control of domestic pipe lines. These considerations are taken into account and dealt with in the bill without introducing a separate licensing procedure.
There is provision in the bill to ensure that a certificate may be suspended or revoked if its terms and conditions are violated or if the operation of the pipe line is conducted in a manner not in compliance with the act, the regulations thereunder, or any lawful order of the board. Finally, the bill provides that a pipe line company may not, without leave of the board, sell, lease, amalgamate or abandon its facilities; a certificate and the


privileges and immunities provided by it, would be transferable only by leave of the board.
The experience of the federal power commission in the United States is that it is unnecessary to issue an operating licence as well as a certificate of public convenience and necessity. In fact the order of the federal power commission approving an application is itself regarded as the certificate of convenience and necessity and is the only authority a pipe line company requires to construct, maintain and operate the facilities specified. There is a separate requirement of a presidential permit to export or import gas, comparable to the proposal in this bill that there continue to be in Canada a separate procedure and licence required in respect of export and import of gas.
In our view no useful purpose will be served by requiring a pipe line company to obtain a licence to operate in addition to a certificate of public convenience and necessity, leave to open and any export or import permit required. To set up two requirements instead of one would tend to add to administrative work without serving any useful purpose. It would seem more or less immaterial whether the basic permission is described as a certificate of public convenience and necessity or as a licence for which the basic consideration would be the public convenience and necessity. By whatever name, one permission should suffice for the purpose specified.
In addition to the certificate procedure for pipe lines which I have been discussing, the bill provides a parallel, though more briefly outlined, set of arrangements for international electrical power lines. Power export licences have been issued in the past under the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importations of Gas Act. The construction of facilities to export power was subject to the same licensing arrangement. What is here intended is to improve the consistency of the statutory requirements by applying the certificate procedure to the construction of the physical facilities to export power, in parallel with the procedure applied to the construction of pipe lines for the export of gas. The export of power will require a licence as before, but it is now to be issued through the same agency and under the same statute that will govern pipe line construction. It is not intended to impose any regulation upon the construction of interprovincial power lines, since most large systems are either provincially owned or under close provincial control and are merely interconnected one with the other.
I come now, Mr. Speaker, to the very important question of the criteria which the bill

will require the board to apply in dealing with applications for certificates of public convenience and necessity for pipe lines and international power lines. In considering what should be specified the government was mindful on the one hand of the possibility that a detailed list of criteria might result in some danger of restrictive interpretation by the courts if they were to take the view that what is not specified may not be taken into account; on the other hand, a too general description might afford insufficient guidance to the board.
The bill will enable the board to consider all such matters as appear to it to be relevant to the question of public convenience and necessity, while at the same time suggesting to the board that it may take into account certain more particular considerations. In wording these considerations we had regard to section 12 (3) of the Pipe Lines Act, recommendation 21 of the Borden report, section 15 (3) of the Aeronautics Act and a set of 24 points which the board of transport commissioners has embodied in a memorandum for its own guidance and for the guidance of applicants in leave to construct proceedings before it.
The part of the bill which has to do with traffic, tolls and tariffs lies at the heart of the legislation and is perhaps the most important single new feature. The Pipe Lines Act provided for the control of the traffic, tolls and tariffs of oil pipe line companies once such companies had been declared by the board of transport commissioners to be common carriers. However, although the major oil pipe lines have in fact acted as common carriers they were never declared by the board to be such, and accordingly their traffic, tolls and tariffs have never been controlled. The charges of gas transmission pipe lines have not been subject to any control.
Gas prices at the point of production are regarded by the provinces of origin as being under their jurisdiction, and gas prices to the ultimate consumer are controlled by the province in which consumption takes place. The government of Canada has had the power to exercise control over the price of gas being exported under the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act. It has long been felt by many people, including the members of this government, that the gap in regulation of the price of gas between the point of first sale and the point of sale to distributors in the area of consumption was a gap which in the public interest should be closed.
The case for regulation of gas transmission charges is fairly straightforward. The commodity which gas transmission companies provide is in competition with other energy
National Energy Board sources, so they are not so clearly in the position of a monoplistic public utility as are, for example, water services. However, few if any of their customers can turn to another source of gas, and if they do turn to another energy source they incur the expense of installing different equipment. The gas transmission companies are therefore in a partial monopoly position, and the public interest requires that they should demonstrate that their rates are not such as to constitute exploitation of that quasi-monopoly position.
At the same time, since they must compete at the point of origin for supplies of gas and compete at the point of sale with other fuels and energy sources, there is a substantial element of risk for gas transmission companies. For this reason they must not be prevented by regulatory action from earning a return sufficient to attract capital, nor must management be deprived of the normal incentive to improve efficiency.
We hold the same view about oil pipe line operations. Here there is the added factor that it is more feasible for the pipe line customers to obtain their oil from other sources. Also, the competition between oil and other fuels is perhaps more intense than the competition faced by gas, and the results of oil pipe line operations are accordingly more subject to fluctuation. Some oil producers can find an outlet to market through only one pipe line, and some refineries are similarly dependent on one pipe line. Oil pipe lines therefore have some of the characteristics of monopoly, and the argument for some regulation in the public interest therefore applies.
Neither in the case of oil pipe lines nor in the case of gas pipe lines will the public gain anything if regulation is so restrictive as to put the pipe lines out of business, or discourage their normal development, or impede the building of new pipe lines to serve new or expanding markets, or restrict the essential work of exploration and discovery of further reserves of oil and gas. Our objective, therefore, is to find the means and level of regulation that will adequately protect the public interest, and particularly the interest of the consumer, while maintaining healthy conditions for the pipe line industry, the oil and gas producing industries and the industries distributing oil products and gas for consumption.
The bill does not specify a formula which the board is to apply in examining and, if need be, in setting tolls and tariffs. On the contrary, we are convinced that it would be an error to crystallize in statutory form a single formula to apply to all the companies in either the oil pipe line or gas pipe line industries. Certainly no single formula would

National Energy Board apply to the two industries, where the nature of business and the inherent risks are so different. The circumstances of individual companies differ widely one from another, and the circumstances of the industries as a whole change so substantially over time that any single rigid formula would be found inappropriate almost before it could be applied.
What is needed here is flexibility combined with an understanding of the industries involved and of the public interests affected. We hope to provide this through a board of competent men, served by well trained and experienced staff, appreciative of the public interest and of the needs and problems of the industries concerned.
This board will, I am sure, in due course draw up and publish a set of rules which will provide a firm framework for rates. It would, however, be unfair to the proposed board, to the industries and to the public to establish at the outset some untested statutory formula which would bind the hands of the board for the future.
This explains why there is not in the bill any reference to the shareholders' equity formula proposed by the Borden commission in its recommendation 12. In fairness to the Borden commission I should like to draw attention at this juncture to a paragraph in its report which has perhaps been overlooked by some of those who have criticized that recommendation. I quote from the report, page 41:
We have carefully considered whether the proposed legislation should fix the rate of return to be allowed on the shareholders' equity and whether this rate might be different in the case of oil or gas pipe lines or, alternatively, whether these matters should be left to the discretion of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. We have concluded that it is preferable to allow the board to exercise its discretion in this regard, recognizing that in so doing it will strive to exercise its powers in a fair manner and authorize rates, and thus a level of earnings, having regard to the circumstances of each case, sufficient to attract the necessary capital. The flexibility which will obtain under such a plan is, in our view, particularly desirable.
Gas transmission pipe line companies buy gas outright at the point of production or processing and sell it outright to their customers. In this they are unlike the oil pipe line companies which in general carry oil owned by either producers or purchasers for a toll which is part of a published tariff. It is not the practice in peacetime to control prices of commodities in internal trade, but it is normal to control transportation or transmission charges, as in the case of railway freight rates. The bill therefore provides for treating as a toll a certain proportion of the difference

between the price paid by the transmission company for the gas and the price charged by the company to its customers. The fixing of this proportion is to be left to the board.
I wish to turn now to the question of exports and imports. The provisions of the bill in this regard will replace the corresponding provisions of the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act, and differ from the latter in several important respects. First, export and import licensing will in future be administered by the national energy board rather than being dealt with by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Second, the statutory provision for the imposition of export duties on electric power laid down in section 4 of the existing act has been omitted from this bill and taken up instead in the Excise Tax Act. Third, the export of oil is no longer to be licensed unless a proclamation to that effect is issued by the governor in council. The licensing of oil imports, which is not regulated under present legislation, may similarly be instituted by proclamation.
It will be noted that the term "fluids" dating back to the original act in 1907, has been omitted from this bill to be replaced by gas and, by proclamation, hydrocarbons which include gas and oil. "Fluids" were defined as gas, oil, water or any other fluids whether liquid or gaseous, that originate or are produced or recovered in Canada. While the export of fluids was defined as their transmission through pipe lines and other like contrivances, the power to license exports of water was not called into use until 1955, when it was used in reference to a power project on the Arrow lakes on the grounds that the weir involved was a "like contrivance". The passing of the International Rivers Improvement Act later that year, however, obviated the need for further control of this sort. Two other fluids, salt in solution and wood pulp in aqueous suspension, were also caught by this definition and brought under licence. Since the intent of this bill is to deal with energy matters and not the incidental use of water as a transporting agent for non-energy commodities, only the export and import of gas, and by proclamation oil, and the export of electric power will be controlled by the proposed legislation.
Perhaps the most important difference is that export and import licences will in future be issued only after public hearing. It has long been a just cause of public complaint that the existing procedure provided no means by which interested parties could appear, be heard, and examine applicants for an export licence, and that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been under no obligation to state what considerations he had before him

in approving or denying a licence. The public hearing process, which in the bill is provided for in that part which deals with the organization of the board, will at once afford better protection to the public interest in these important decisions, and a more satisfactory way of dealing with applications from the point of view of the government and of the various parties concerned.
It is intended that the governor in council's approval of export and import licences, and of their cancellation or suspension, will be required. This will be expressed in the regulations. One such regulation will be that no licence for the export of gas or power or the import of gas will be valid without the approval of the governor in council. The reason for this approach is that in the event it is decided to put into effect the proposed permissive power to license imports and exports of oil, it would be undesirable to make every licence for every import of oil affected dependent upon approval of the governor in council.
The term of export licences is not to exceed 25 years. This upper limit is regarded as the term likely to be required to enable financing of gas export pipe lines. It is intended to continue the policy of limiting electric power export licences to one year, unless exceptional circumstances justify a longer term.
Before issuing an export licence for gas or electric power, the board would have to be satisfied on the reasonableness of the price to be obtained. The attempt to reconcile exports and domestic price which was expressed in regulation 9 under the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act has proved inadequate, since the conditions specified were found never to exist. As in the case of rate regulation, it was the conclusion of the government that any rigid statutory formula would probably be more harmful than helpful. The price and other considerations which the board is to apply to export applications are therefore expressed broadly. The principles will be that quantities to be exported should not exceed the surplus remaining of proven and potential reserves after allowance for reasonably foreseeable Canadian requirements, and that the export price should be just and reasonable in relation to the public interest.
The matter of import and export restrictions with regard to oil requires some particular attention. The measure now before us provides that the application of that part of the bill dealing with exports and imports may, by proclamation of the governor in council, be extended to oil.
National Energy Board
I shall first deal briefly with exports of oil. Under the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act, exports of oil require a licence, which in the case of oil pipe lines has been freely granted on an annual basis. So far as I can determine, the licensing requirement was applied by an analogy with the reasons for regulating exports of power and gas. The analogy is not valid, because oil, unlike power and gas, is a commodity moving fairly freely in world trade, moving from a variety of sources to a given market or from a given source to a variety of markets, and moving by various means of transport, of which pipe lines and water-borne tankers are the most economical.
Gas and power, by contrast, move by fixed channels under long term contracts at the source and long term contracts in the area of consumption, so that once committed to a market they cannot be withdrawn without hardship. A gas export service once established must continue for a substantial period to enable the enterprise to attract capital in the first place, and to permit amortization of the necessary investment. Interruption of such export service is apt to be a source of international friction. Hence there is a clear case for being cautious about permitting exports of any power or gas which we are likely to require ourselves, but with respect to oil these conditions do not apply.
As in the case of other important products moving in trade, our interest and the interest of the industry is to sell oil where we can, either within or outside of Canada. Therefore we feel there is no requirement of national policy to be served at present by licensing exports of oil. On the contrary, we have only recently been successful in obtaining exemption from the restrictions imposed by the United States on oil imports, and it would ill accord with the treatment we are now receiving from the United States to establish new restrictions on the export of oil.
The case with respect to licensing of imports of oil is different and more complicated. I do not propose to argue that case fully today. It would be premature to do so until the second report of the Borden commission in respect of this matter has been received and considered.
There are, however, certain obvious considerations to be kept in mind. I referred a moment ago to the recently announced exemption by the United States from its import controls of crude oil, unfinished oils and petroleum products moving into the United States by pipe line, rail or motor carrier. Canada is the principal beneficiary of this arrangement, which will improve our exports of crude oil and will also restore the less

National Energy Board important but still significant export trade we have been building up in refined products and in liquefied petroleum gases. In the light of this favourable outcome of our negotiations with the United States, it would seem unwise at the present moment to take any action by way of import controls which might give rise to misunderstanding and possibly call the present arrangement into question.
Some persons have recently been inclined to minimize the importance of these United States exemptions. Actually the prospects for increasing our exports of oil are very encouraging. In the Puget sound market, where there are three large refineries which are logical customers for Canadian oil moving through the Trans Mountain pipe line, the July purchases nominated by General Petroleums will, I understand, rise from 15,000 barrels per day to 27,000 barrels per day; those of Shell from 12,000 to 20,000 barrels per day, and those of the Texas Company from nothing to 8,000 barrels per day, a total increase from 27,000 barrels to 55,000 barrels per day or an almost immediate doubling of our sales in this natural export market for Canadian oil.
There are many other considerations important to this question of imported oil, and particularly its relevance to our general commercial policy and trade relations with other countries. The government has been weighing these considerations, and will continue to do so.
Last Monday evening the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) referred to certain doubts he had about the proposal to give the governor in council power to impose by proclamation licensing requirements on the imports and exports of oil. His reservations were on two scores. The first-and these are his words which are to be found at page 3783 of Hansard-was this:
-that this is a matter of such importance and of such a nature that it should be dealt with by parliament and not be taken to the governor in council by way of arbitrary authority.
His second point-and again I quote his own words-was this:
-so long as that power is contained in the legislation, then we are going to have a situation where a threat is going to be hanging over the heads of the industry at large that the board will interfere by way of regulation, and that is damaging because of recommendation 19 of the Borden commission report.
I would assure the hon. member and the house that these points have indeed been taken into account by the government in preparing the bill, and that only after careful thought have we come to the conclusion that in the present circumstances the merits of

the course we propose must outweigh the disadvantages to which he has referred.
He is quite right in thinking that some uncertainty will remain but it is not, however, the threat of frivolous or unnecessary government intervention. It is the threat that the present world-wide conditions of surplus supply which exist in the oil industry will result in so great a decline in world prices, and such great pressure of supplies of oil offered at distress prices, that normal marketing arrangements may be overwhelmed. If this were to happen, very serious injury could be caused to the oil producing and processing industries in this country.
It is against this contingency that we consider it necessary to take the power under discussion. If the need arose it would in all probability arise quickly, and would require quick action to avert serious disruption. For this reason it is proposed to make the power applicable by proclamation.

speechtext:
In view of the length of the (b) part of recommendation 19, after the hon. member has had an opportunity of contributing to the discussion and when we reach the conclusion of the debate I might comment on that point and others that he may raise.
I should now like to deal with the limitations upon the authority of the board. The bill does not give the board any power to regulate coal, atomic energy or uranium, or matters having to do with electrical power except for export of such power. Neither does the bill propose any alteration of the arrangements under which our negotiations with the United States for a mutually satisfactory program of development of the Columbia river basin are being conducted, though I am sure those who are now involved in those negotiations on the Canadian side will look to the board when it is established for co-operation and assistance. While the board's advisory functions require that it be free to study any aspect of energy, we do not believe it would be profitable under present circumstances to disrupt the existing agencies involved in these related fields.

Great care has been taken to ensure that in its vital actions, particularly as to certificates of public convenience and necessity, import and export licences, and the establishment of regulations, the board must have the approval of the governor in council. This is intended to ensure that the decisions of the board which affect the national interest are consistent with general government policy. At the same time we have sought to assure the security of tenure and independence of the board and its staff. This balance between independence and responsibility to parliament is always somewhat difficult to achieve; we believe that here we have proposed a satisfactory equilibrium.
While we have sought to arrange that the findings of the board shall be final, as should be the factual findings of any expert board, we have been careful to preserve the right of the citizen to appeal to the highest courts of the land on matters of law and jurisdiction. Also, I would emphasize again that we have sought with great care to avoid any interference with the proper jurisdiction of the provinces.
Throughout this statement I have indicated our desire to strike a balance in discharging our responsibilities between, on the one hand, the public interest in the sound development and use for the benefit of the people of Canada of our vast and vital energy resources and, on the other hand, the essential requirement that enterprise be left free to make its own decisions so far as may be consistent with that public interest. The functions performed by the energy and related industries are of great importance to the well-being of our country, and we do not wish to hamper or impair the ability of these industries to perform their services. Hence we have drafted a bill which is general rather than particular in respect of formulae to be applied in regulation, because only through stating our intentions in somewhat general terms can we preserve that flexibility which we feel is essential.
Finally, may I point out that we have attempted to arrange that the transition from the present situation to that envisaged under the bill can be accomplished without delay, disruption of activity, or duplication of effort. We have sought to provide that the existing rights of companies which will be under the jurisdiction of the board will be fully protected in so far as is consistent with such new functions as rate regulation. We have provided for time within which such companies can accommodate themselves to the new statute, and have sought to avoid placing a sudden and difficult burden of requirements upon them. We have provided 66968-9-250
National Energy Board that matters now before the board of transport commissioners under the Pipe Lines Act, and matters now before the Minister of Trade and Commerce under the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act, shall be transferred to a similar position before the new board without loss of status or repetition of effort.
The house will decide the nature and extent of the debate on this major issue which is of such importance for Canada's future. I hope that full discussion will result in complete clarification of a subject that is not devoid of complications. At the committee stage there will be an opportunity of considering the details. The general principles I have attempted to set out today. This bill, if enacted, will set the pattern for the development and use, in the national interest, of the great resources of energy which are the endowment of our country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has placed some interesting information on the record. We are grateful to him for having done so. The large amount of information he has decided to place on the record is a good indication of how important this proposed legislation is.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, after reading or hearing the remarks made in the house last Monday by the minister, when he had the responsibility of moving that legislation be introduced to establish a national energy board, one might have wondered whether the government intended to incorporate in such legislation a large proportion, if not all, of the main recommendations found in the interim report submitted by the Borden commission on energy. Indeed, the minister himself, in the debate on the resolution, after briefly commending the commission for the conscientious discharge of its heavy responsibilities, made this specific statement:
Many of its recommendations are to be implemented as will be clear when the bill is before the house.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we have gained a quite different impression now that we had a chance to take a good look at the contents of the bill. We now feel that the government has been prompted by many other authors than those of the preliminary Borden report.
Everything in this bill which might be considered consistent and sound has been borrowed from the pipe lines act, from the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation

National Energy Board of Gas Act, from the Railway Act, and, I would even say, from various recommendations made late in 1957 in the final report prepared by the Gordon commission on Canada's economic prospects.
Mr. Speaker, all essential parts of the bill are borrowed from the various acts just mentioned and from recommendations which are exactly similar to those of the Gordon commission. The non-essential parts, those that are contentious or even prejudicial to our industry or to the public interest are the government's own ideas or have been suggested by the Borden commission report.
I shall come back to this point a little later in my remarks, and we also shall have the opportunity of emphasizing what I just said when the house sits in committee on the various sections of the bill.
Mr. Speaker, in a detailed study of power prospects in Canada, prepared and edited at the urgent request of the Gordon commission by Mr. John Davis, who is an expert in this field, we find abundant information on this country's hydraulic resources, on coal, oil, natural gas, nuclear energy, as well as on tidal and solar energy.
For the first time in Canada, a complete study of mutual relations between the various power industries has been made in the said document by that great expert, Mr. Davis. That study enables us to form some estimation of the rate of growth of Canada's power requirements in the next 20 or 30 years, and of the changes that will occur in the consumption of the various forms of energy and in the relative contribution of various power resources to satisfy the needs of the country. I might add that if this government had really sought to be consistent and had tried to act as promptly as had been implied, it would have gone ahead, on the basis of this survey, and would immediately have established a national energy board, in the fall of 1957 or early in 1958.
The Davis study is divided in three parts:
(a)	Energy consumption and economic growth;
(b)	The energy supplying industries;
(c)	Energy and Canada's economic prospects.
In part (a), or first part, in chapter 2 dealing with energy consumption and economic expansion, we read the following on page 19:
Canada's industrial expansion in the 20th century can be interpreted not only in monetary terms hut

also by listing the ever increasing quantities of energy being put to use on the nation's farms, in its mines, stores, and factories, and in its homes. With the labour force today only little more than twice as large as that of 50 years ago but with better equipment, improved techniques, and-more significant still-with the help of about five times as much energy, the Canadian economy is turning out about six times as many goods and services as it was producing in 1900.
Scarcely a field of endeavour but has benefited in one way or another from the increased availability of fuel and power. Today a farmer with power-driven equipment can harvest 30 acres of wheat for every acre he could have reaped a century ago, using hand tools.
Each paper mill operator is turning out ten times as much newsprint as his forebears did around the turn of the century. To raise a ton of ore, the average miner took about two hours as recently as 1930, less than 50 minutes in 1955. Distance has become less of a handicap. On the railways, the latest diesel electric locomotive is capable of doing five times as much work as its steam driven counterpart at the end of world war II.
The report goes on to explain the great advantages of certain power resources we have here in Canada.
In part (b) of the Davis study dealing with energy supplying industries, the author has compiled a great variety of information on each of those industries.
In regard to the oil industry, for instance, Mr. Davis first makes an historical summary; he gives an outline of the world situation, deals with the prospects of Canadian oil and concludes by outlining a long-term program.
In the case of the natural gas industry, after outlining its background and dealing with prospective markets for Canadian gas, Mr. Davis explains the supply and demand pattern and gives details on its financing and development.
Canada is exceptionally well endowed with water power resources. Being both large and conveniently located they have played a major role in its economic development. Among other things they have helped to make up for a lack of mineral fuels in central Canada. They have made possible the processing of forest, mineral and other primary products on a scale unmatched anywhere else in the world. And, by making low-cost electrical energy available to the nation's homes, farms, stores, offices and factories, they have contributed in innumerable ways to the exceptionally high standard of living which Canadians now enjoy.
A little further on, the report says:
Thanks to a favourable climate and to the right kind of topography, to widespread precipitation, extensive drainage basins and readily harnessed water power sites, Canada has made tremendous strides in this important energy field. With the exception of the United States, this country has installed more hydro capacity than any other nation in the world. While Norway's per capita installation still tops the list at 1.6 horsepower, Canada is second with 1.1 horsepower, followed in order by Switzerland and Sweden.
There again, the report gives very instructive and important information. Later on,

on page 201, Mr. Davis concludes that part of his report by saying:
Whatever happens, Canada's power industry will continue to grow both in extent and complexity. Accelerating as it does, it will help through its very momentum, to carry along with it the rest of the Canadian economy. Thus, in innumerable and in unforeseen ways it will continue to do what it has done so well before-that is to stimulate industrial development in those resources and allied fields where Canadians as a people possess their greatest natural advantage.
Those, sir, are the few paragraphs which I wanted to quote from the Davis study. Considered as a whole, that study is a precious source of statistical information of all kinds and there is no doubt that the government might well have sought inspiration from it and from the final report of the Gordon commission on Canada's economic prospects before submitting some legislation which would have met the demands of industry while ensuring the Canadian people of the best possible use of this country's power resources.
The final report of the Gordon commission was submitted in November 1957-a very significant date to keep in mind. Giving an overall picture of our power needs and resources the commission sums up the position as follows, as appears on page 143 of the report:
Issues of this kind, in our opinion, should be examined within a context broad enough to include all forms of energy and all the energy industries. In this chapter, we have tried to suggest that, although there are a number of separate energy industries, the interrelations between them are close and complex. Each of the various energy resources has its own peculiar advantages which make it better suited than others for some purposes. Wood needs no processing before it can be burned as a fuel and is found almost everywhere, except on the prairies, so that it will still be used for heating in some outlying districts, although Canada's total consumption of fuel wood will continue to decline. Coal has both a high heat content and valuable metallurgical properties, and there are large reserves of it. It will continue to be essential in steel making and, after the passage of time, may begin to recapture some of the volume markets that it is now in the process of losing.
That is what we hope, Mr. Speaker.
Petroleum products provide the most practical form of power for cars and trucks, and highway traffic will continue to depend on it almost exclusively. Natural gas is a particularly clean and convenient fuel and its special properties will always ensure for it many premium markets. During the 1957 election campaign, Mr. Speaker-and this has been mentioned very often in this chamber-the Prime Minister promised the Canadian people quick and bold action on this matter. The Conservative party was going to encourage through specific measures, a greater degree of Canadian ownership in this field and the further processing in Canada of raw materials and by-products through the more efficient development and use of our sources of energy.
I would like to quote from the remarks made by the Prime Minister in Toronto on February 4, 1957, at the annual dinner of the Toronto board of trade. Of course that was some time before the election of 1957. However, this is what the Prime Minister said:
There is a need now for the setting up of a Canadian national energy board, with its membership composed of technical personnel, who might be selected by the president of the national research council of business organizations, of the dominion and provincial governments, to the end that the most effective use of the energy resources of Canada, in the interests of the public welfare, may be assured. We have vast resources of gas and oil and coal and uranium. I believe the time has come to set up such a board, whose duty it would be to advise and to recommend proposals regarding these resources, so that they may be safeguarded from prejudicial action now, ill-timed action to the detriment of this and future generations.
What was the situation in this respect after the general election and during the fall session of 1957? Did the government take action at that time, as was urgently required by our industry and as had been promised-that is the point-to Canadians? No, Mr. Speaker; it merely submitted the recommendation of the Gordon commission to another royal commission created for that purpose.
What did we on this side of the house have to say then about the creation of the Borden commission? Here is, for instance, what Hon. Jean Lesage, the former minister of northern affairs and national resources, had to say on November 13, 1957, at page 1082 of Hansard:
In the field of energy, here, again, we have heard no policy announced by this government. We all know that the Gordon commission devoted a good deal of attention to this problem and will in its

This is what can be called quick action, but what about the wisdom of the action. Of course, everybody knows why this royal commission on energy was appointed; everyone in Canada knows that it is to hide the fact that the Conservative party wants to continue the pipe line policy initiated by the past Liberal government.
Mr. Lesage continued:
That is why the royal commission on energy has been appointed. The Conservatives strongly criticized this policy of the past Liberal government and of course they do not dare admit publicly now the fact that they endorse the policy. What they wish to do is hide that policy of theirs behind a royal commission. They do not have the courage to admit they will have to follow our policy in this matter. They intend to escape their responsibility by appointing a royal commission.
What did we on this side of the house have to say about the creation of that royal commission? We said what Mr. Lesage said in the remarks 1 have just quoted.
In the fall of 1957, therefore, we on this side of the house contended that the appointment of the Borden commission was a means of shelving problems and a mere delaying tactic to enable the government to postpone taking a definite stand and specific action before the forthcoming election of 1958, That delaying tactic has worked. After a year of inquiry the Borden commission presented its first report in October, 1958. That report contained final recommendations only in so far as natural gas is concerned. We all recall also how widely that report and some of its sections in particular were criticized when the report was made public.
Then more delays were experienced. It was only on April 23, six months after the government had received the report, that a resolution appeared on the order paper. But again nothing happened. It was only after another month that the government decided at last to proceed with the resolution. The bill was made available to us for study only on Tuesday evening. Finally, after all these delays and hesitation and confusion, the government discovered that this was a most urgent matter and that the house should proceed with the consideration of the 101 provisions of the bill without any adequate time to study them carefully.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, I must say here that we are grateful to the Prime Minister for agreeing on Wednesday to postpone second reading of the bill until today.
National Energy Board During the intervening hours we have had some time to study the bill, and for this reason we think this was a good move on the part of the Prime Minister, because it will accelerate debate at this stage.
We think this is an important piece of legislation. It is a long and complex bill which could have deep, long term implications on the future economic development of Canada. For this reason and also because of the long delays in bringing the legislation before the house, for which the government must assume full responsibility, we on this side of the house want to make clear that we are far from being satisfied about the haste shown by the government on this occasion. We claim that not enough time has been provided to hon. members for full consideration and study of the bill. We also believe that those individuals and groups more immediately concerned with this matter will not be able to analyse the legislation and make their views known in so short a period of time.
In the little time I have had to study the bill, however, I have been able to discover that this legislation is almost a complete repudiation of the Borden report. I am quite sure that no other royal commission has been more completely ignored and by-passed. This shows very clearly how right we were in the fall of 1957 when we claimed that the setting up of the royal commission was merely a delaying tactic used by the government to postpone action until after the 1958 election.
The bill we are now considering is not only a repudiation of the recommendations of the Borden commission but is also a repudiation of the definite promises and commitments made by the Conservative party to the Canadian people before the 1957 election. Most of the provisions of the bill are not new, as we intend to show at the committee stage when we will be able to consider the bill in detail. A great number of its sections have been taken without any change or without any substantial modification from the Pipe Lines Act and from the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act, as I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks in French.
The bill also contains a few new provisions which we think are clearly undesirable. It gives unnecessarily wide powers to the governor in council. This is surprising from a government which when in opposition was so critical of government by order in council. I should like at this stage to

Mr. Speaker, just before the house rose at one o'clock I was commenting on clause 87 of the bill, and I was telling the house that the Borden commission had been placed in an impossible and untenable position by the government. This is not the whole story, however, Mr. Speaker. According to this bill, the legislative provisions with respect to oil, after having been approved by parliament, will be implemented only if and when the government so wishes. This, Mr. Speaker, is legislation by cabinet and we certainly cannot accept such a procedure. We maintain that if and when the government feels legislative action is necessary with respect to oil it should then, but only then, ask parliament to take such action. The government is certainly not entitled at this stage to seek these wide powers when it does not even know how it will use them in the future.
Another illustration of government by order in council is provided by clause 85,

paragraph 2, which enables the government to exempt any person, any product, any transaction and any area from the legislative provisions and regulations regarding export and import of power or hydrocarbons. This is another example of the wide, arbitrary power that the government is seeking in this bill. Parliament is asked to enact legislation and, at the same time, to authorize the government to exempt from the legislation all the possible cases which could be covered by it. We certainly cannot accept provisions which give such wide powers to the government.
Our attitude toward this bill is clear and simple. We approve its principle, which is to set up a national energy board. As a matter of fact, we have been in favour of such a board since January, 1958, at least. I should like, at this stage, to quote from the resolution approved by the Liberal party at the last convention in Ottawa, in January 1958 and which I quoted on Monday evening, May 18, 1959, as reported at page 3773 of Hansard for that date,
We of the Liberal party advocate the integrated development in co-operation with the provinces of petroleum, natural gas, hydroelectric power, coal and all other energy sources across the whole of Canada to meet the needs of industrial and population growth. We advocate the establishment of a national energy authority to advise the government as to the long term requirements of energy in Canada, including the best methods of providing efficient long term uses in Canada and for export.
Therefore, in 1958 we were on record as favouring such a board, and this is long before the government decided to introduce the present bill. However, we do not want another board which will more or less duplicate what has already been done by other existing government agencies, and thus create further administrative delays and confusion. From this point of view, we feel that the functions of the board have not been clearly defined in relation to the responsibilities of existing agencies.
It is true that this morning the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) gave some information to the house on this subject. However, I should like to outline a few of the problems we will have on our hands if this division of responsibility is not made absolutely clear. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has failed, in that way, to tell us what will happen to the present agencies established under statutes of this parliament and operating within the field of energy. He said this morning that these agencies would continue to work, but we should have had more information regarding this problem. This question, of such fundamental importance, was almost ignored. Will these present agencies, and their functions, be integrated within

the framework established for the new national energy board? The minister should be more definite about that. Will certain parts of present agencies be brought under the aegis of the new authority, or will complete existing agencies be incorporated? Parliament should have such information.
It may be that all present agencies will be maintained-we were not given this understanding this morning-without any changes in their functions. If that is the arrangement contemplated, we are entitled to ask how the new board will discharge the duties assigned to it in the bill and still avoid extensive and inefficient duplication with existing machinery of government?

As a matter of fact, to a very large extent the future industrial life of Canada as well as the prosperity of Canadians generally depend upon the availability of cheap energy sources. It has become clear in very recent years that Canada has large supplies of natural gas and petroleum. We are an industrial nation, and we in the C.C.F. believe it is within the capabilities of the Canadian nation to develop our energy 66968-9-251
National Energy Board resources at low cost, and be able to provide this energy to Canadian industry and consumers.
It is on that basis that we approach the subject and the bill now under discussion. Mr. Speaker, this whole field was the subject of a very important inquiry by the Borden royal commission on energy. This inquiry took some considerable time. It cost the taxpayers of this country a great deal of money, and an exhaustive study has been made. As a matter of fact, in a return brought down in this house on February 25, it was shown that the cost of this royal commission has amounted to $317,124.52. It is therefore correct to say that the Canadian nation has invested a large sum of money in the inquiry that was made, and the recommendations that have been presented to parliament should be given every consideration.
Mr. Speaker, as I read this report and its recommendations, I think that some of the most important recommendations are contained in the list of recommendations and the suggested amendments to the Pipe Lines Act. Recommendation No. 11, paragraph (c) reads as follows:
It shall be mandatory for the board of transport commissioners for Canada to regulate the prices or rates of gas pipe line companies subject to the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, and, in so doing, to require, if necessary, any such gas pipe line company to renegotiate the terms of any existing contracts for the sale or delivery of gas for distribution or consumption within Canada;
Paragraph (d) reads as follows:
It shall be mandatory for the board of transport commissioners for Canada periodically, and at least once in every 24-month period during the early years of regulation, to review and, if deemed necessary, to adjust the prices, tolls, rates and tariffs of pipe line companies regulated by it;
This report refers to the board of transport commissioners. We do not quarrel with the fact that the government has decided to give these powers now held by the board of transport commissioners in this connection to the energy board. We feel that the recommendations apply equally to the powers that will be held by the energy board as they should apply to the powers now held by the board of transport commissioners.
Recommendation No. 12 reads as follows:
That the prices, tolls, rates or tariffs of a company owning or operating an oil or gas pipe line, as regulated by the board of transport commissioners for Canada, should be just and reasonable, non-discriminatory and calculated to yield a fair rate of return on the shareholders' equity, after making due allowance for reasonable and proper operating expenses, depreciation, interest, income and other taxes.
Mr. Speaker, the recommendations contained herein are very clear. They ask that power be exercised by a board to regulate the prices or rates of gas pipe line companies

National Energy Board subject to the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada and in bringing about these rates to require, if necessary, any gas pipe line company to renegotiate the terms of any existing contracts for the sale or delivery of gas or its distribution or consumption within Canada. The purpose of this section is to remove any injustice that presently is contained in the rates charged for gas in terms of distribution or consumption.
It is further recommended that at least every 24 months it shall be mandatory for the board to review and, if deemed necessary, to adjust the prices, tolls, rates and tariffs of pipe line companies regulated by it. These recommendations are that the board have wide powers and that the board must use those powers to set tolls and to regulate the prices of gas and oil.
The other recommendation to which I have referred was to the effect that the prices, tolls, rates or tariffs of the companies owning and operating an oil or gas pipe line shall be so regulated and calculated as to yield a fair rate of return on the shareholders' equity after having made due allowance for reasonable and proper operating expenses, depreciation, interest, income and other taxes. This is a most important recommendation. The whole purpose behind this recommendation is to remove from the calculations of cost the fabulous profits that have been made by investors and the controllers of gas and oil pipe lines in this country. This recommendation says that anyone who has invested money in these companies should receive a fair return on his equity. The purpose is to provide that Canadian industries and consumers will not be saddled with the high rates for energy that are necessary to pay large returns on the highly speculative and bloated profits and income that accrue to the controllers of the gas and oil industry.
These are the central recommendations and these are the recommendations the government has avoided. It is true that by this bill the government is setting up a board but the board is free to do almost anything it likes and indeed it is free to fold its arms if it so wishes and do almost nothing.
