The board may disallow any tariff or any portion thereof that it considers to be contrary to any of the provisions of this act or to any order of the board, and may require a company, within a prescribed time, to substitute a tariff satisfactory to the board in lieu thereof, or may prescribe other tariffs in lieu of the tariff or portion thereof so disallowed.
The board has full discretion to sit on its hands indefinitely and let the speculators and buccaneers continue to make large and

bloated profits from Canadian industry and consumers. That is the attitude of the government. The policy of the government has been to forget all of its statements in the past and to forget its well-known position that Canadian interests should be protected and Canadian energy resources should be developed by Canadian capital in the interests of Canadians. The government has forsaken that position and introduced this anaemic bill to set up a board the powers of which are not well defined and by this means to allow the exploitation of Canadian energy resources in the future and to allow them to remain in the hands of outside interests and overnight buccaneers and to remove these resources from direct and precise control by a board operating in the interests of this nation.
The royal commission on energy was instructed to inquire into this whole general field to see to what extent speculative and exorbitant profits had been made in this industry in the past. The commission has done a most thorough job in this regard. It inquired into the whole operation of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. I am convinced from reading the report that it was precisely because of the huge profits that had been made by a few people on almost negligible investments that the royal commission recommended that the people of Canada should not have to pay rates for gas and oil that provide fabulous returns on such investments.
We have heard a lot about Texas buccaneers from hon. gentlemen opposite in times gone by. This commission inquired into the extent to which Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited is controlled by outside sources. On page 74 of the report it is stated that as of June 1, 1958 the company that held the second largest number of shares in Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited was Canadian Delhi Oil Limited, Calgary, Alberta which had 542,885 shares. Looking further into the affairs of Canadian Delhi Oil Limited the commission at page 77 of the report had this to say:
The commission has been advised that Mrs. Betty Lee Moor MacGuire, who was the registered owner at the date above referred to of 238,984 common shares of Canadian Delhi Oil Ltd., is a daughter of Mr. Lee Moor, an associate of Clinton W. Murchison of Dallas, Texas; that the partnership of Richardson & Bass, shown as the registered owner of 132,010 common shares, includes as a partner Mr. S. W. Richardson, a Texas independent oil operator, who is likewise shown as being the registered owner in his own name of 35,762 common shares of Canadian Delhi Oil Ltd. and that Clinton W. Murchison, Jr., and John Dabney Murchison, of Dallas, Texas, shown as the registered owners of 275,512 and 229,325 common shares respectively of Canadian Delhi Oil Ltd., are sons of Clinton W. Murchison, Sr., of Dallas, Texas.
Here is concrete evidence of the activities of Texas buccaneers to which the Prime

Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made reference in this house a few years ago. This is evidence of the extent to which Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited is controlled by people living in the United States.
With respect to profits that have been made on certain transactions the commission at pages 82 and 83 of its report had this to say:
Public financing of Trans-Canada was announced in February, 1957. The prospectus of the company is dated February 13, 1957. On February 1, 1957, Mr. Tanner exercised his option with respect to
15.000	shares and on February 6, 1957, with respect to 40,000 shares. As at June 1, 1958, Mr. Tanner held 30,800 of these shares, having transferred
15.000	shares principally to members of his family and 200 shares to the National Trust Company Limited, under a trust agreement, and having sold 9,000 shares for an aggregate price of approximately $263,400. As at the same time, there remained, 5,000 shares with respect to which Mr. Tanner was entitled to exercise his option before March 9, 1959.
Mr. Tanner under his agreement was obligated to pay to Trans-Canada for the 55,000 shares the sum of $440,000. At the middle of September,
1958,	common shares of Trans-Canada were traded on the Toronto stock exchange at approximately $34.50 per share. Had Mr. Tanner retained these optioned shares and sold them at that time and at that price he would have made an apparent capital gain of approximately $1,457,500. This calculation does not take into account the 10,000 shares optioned to him by Canadian Delhi Oil Limited and the western group at $1 per share, which as previously stated he transferred to Mrs. Tanner. In addition, as noted above, Mr. Tanner still has the right, exercisable before March 9,
1959,	to purchase an additional 5,000 shares of Trans-Canada at $8 per share.
Here is a man, Mr. Speaker who according to the royal commission on energy, a commission which cost the Canadian taxpayer over $300,000, who by way of an option and by no risk investment himself, stood to make in September of 1958, with shares at the price of $34.50, a capital gain of $1,457,500. This is the nefarious deal to which the Conservative members used to refer. This is the great betrayal under which one man has made $1,457,500 at the expense of the Canadian nation.
This deal was made, prior to this government coming into office, but what has been the attitude of this government? To set up a royal commission, yes, and a royal commission which brought in a report and said in effect that gas rates should not be set and oil rates should not be set at prices to give this man a $1,457,500 capital gain, but only a return on the equity that he has in the company. This, Mr. Speaker, is the recommendation of the commission and this is the recommendation that this government has refused to follow.
It was not only Mr. Tanner who made a fabulous profit. There was Mr. Charles S.
66968-9-251J
National Energy Board Coates, of Houston, Texas, who himself had a very large option and has made very fabulous profits. The royal commission at page 85 had this to say:
As previously mentioned, public financing of Trans-Canada was announced in February, 1957, and the prospectus with respect to such financing is dated February 13, 1957. On February 11, 1957, Mr. Coates exercised his option in full. As at February 19, 1958, Mr. Coates still held 40,000 of these shares, having sold 10,000 shares in the fall of 1957 for an aggregate price of approximately $280,000. Accordingly, if one takes the price at which common shares of Trans-Canada were traded on the Toronto stock exchange in the middle of September, 1958, i.e. approximately $34.50 per share, and had Mr. Coates retained these 50.000 optioned shares and sold them at that time and at that price, he would have made an apparent capital gain of approximately $1,325,000.
This is another example of the fabulous profits that have been made at the expense of the Canadian nation because of the former government's pipe line action with regard to Trans-Canada pipe line. These are examples of fabulous profits that have been made by certain people connected with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. Look into any major gas company, look into any gas pipe line company in Canada, look into the financial picture of any major oil pipe line in Canada, and you are almost certain to find a duplication of the same kind of fabulous profits.
An inquiry was made into profits that resulted from the operation of the Northern Ontario Natural Gas Company. In the Globe and Mail of Friday, February 13, one finds the report that Mr. Farris purchased 37,500 shares for $300. He sold 22,500 of these shares for $318,300. He retained 15,000 shares, and at the price of approximately $14 per share at which shares are being traded today, this Mr. Farris, on an investment of $300, has a capital gain of $528,000. These are the very kind of fabulous actions that this government is protecting by this legislation in the rates which can be charged which will give a return on these fabulous amounts. Mr. Clark, another investor in the same company, purchased 58,549 shares for $9,072.50. He sold 30,149 shares for $146,215. He retained 28,400 shares, and on the basis of today's trading price this man, on a purchase investment of $9,072.50, is in a position to make $543,000. Mr. Newell, the third person mentioned, purchased 29,334 shares for $10,160. He sold 22,850 shares for $234,125. He still holds 6,548 shares. Mr. Newell, on an investment of just over $10,000, stands to gain $326,000.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, this kind of fabulous profits, based not on risk investment but on mere token investment, based mainly on the control and the acquisition and ownership of large numbers of shares, is a disgrace to this

National Energy Board nation and to this parliament. Because of these fabulous profits, because a few people have control of those great energy resources, the Canadian people have looked to this government to take action to restore the natural resources to the people of this country. This has not been done. As a matter of fact, effective steps to restore control over final charges are not being undertaken by this measure.
In recent elections the government made very strong statements to the people of Canada as to how it would develop resources in the interests of the Canadian people. In a pamphlet published by Progressive Conservative party national headquarters, 141 Laurier avenue west, Ottawa, Ontario prior to the 1957 election this was stated on page six:
Canadian subsidiaries of foreign concerns should be required to provide a substantial interest in their equity stock to Canadian investors.
There is no such reference in this bill. On page seven of the same pamphlet I find these words:
In his opening campaign speech on April 25 John Diefenbaker emphatically stated: "In common with all Canadians, and I underline what I am about to say, we welcome foreign investment. We do not want to see it discouraged. But, I say this-as Canadians a sense of national destiny for Canada calls for that investment being directed to the maximum benefit for Canada. I go farther than that-I quote the words of the Financial Post, which I have referred to, when it said this"-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Before the hon. member goes further with that, would he think that this debate, which is undoubtedly a broad one, deals with foreign investment? It seems to me that it deals with investment in oil, gas and energy companies but it deals with that not as foreign and domestic but as investment. I just wonder whether there are not some limits to the scope of what is relevant in this debate.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I would refer you, Mr. Speaker, to the debate on the trans-Canada pipe line. That was legislation that affected only Canadian pipe lines. Yet a large part of the debate ranged around whether or not the people investing in and controlling that company were in fact Canadians. When we are considering a bill which contains power to control gas prices in this country I think whether the bill is effective depends to some extent on whether the great gas and oil companies that this legislation seeks to control are dominated by outside capital. If we were dealing purely with domestic investors we might have one attitude toward the bill but because we are dealing in fact with an industry which to a very substantial extent is controlled outside this country we have a different attitude to the measure. I feel that
[Mr. Argued
it is exceedingly pertinent to the whole question of the government's energy policy whether or not the companies that may be controlled are themselves owned by and in the control of outside interests.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I think the hon. member has a point with respect to existing companies but what I was endeavouring to find an answer to was whether the general policy of foreign investment was involved in this debate. It seemed to me that the quotations he was using were directed toward foreign investment generally. If he wishes to talk about foreign investment in the existing companies which will come under the control of this legislation that may be all right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: If you will recall, just a moment before I had quoted from the royal commission report as to the fabulous profits made by Mr. Coates of Houston, Texas.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I made no objection to that. I was simply trying to keep the member away from a general discussion of foreign investment in Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
After having referred to
Mr. Coates, after having referred to the royal commission's statement about these people, most of whom are Texans, who control Canadian Delhi Oil Company, I then came to the statement of the Prime Minister as to how this type of foreign investment and control was detrimental to the very existence of this nation. I intend to keep my remarks related to the gas and oil pipe line business but I also have referred to the way these pipe lines are controlled in large measure outside this country. The statement of the Financial Post, and it is a short one, which the Prime Minister quoted was as follows:
How long, with the growing dominance of foreign owned enterprises, Canada can continue a separate existence is the problem before Canada today.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: In my view that general field is too broad a field for this debate and I think the hon. member should keep his remark related to the oil and gas industry.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am dealing with the oil and gas business and the way it is dominated and controlled outside this country and the fact that it is necessary for the government to take action to control the Texas buccaneers. The people and corporations who were once referred to as the pampered pets of the Right Hon. C. D. Howe and who are the pampered pets of this government today, these Texas buccaneers, must be smiling. They must have very broad smiles on their faces because I am sure that when this government took office there was some concern that the party now in power meant to do exactly what it

said it would do, restore control of these companies to Canadians and take action to see that Canadian resources are developed and used by Canadians in the interests of this country.
The government went so far as to appoint a royal commission on which more than $300,000 was spent. It brought in specific recommendations as to how gas and oil going through pipe lines should be controlled but the government has decided to set aside its main recommendations.
The Liberal party appears to be taking a very active part in this debate and I am certain we are going to have many speeches from members of the Liberal party before the debate is over. But I wonder where their basic quarrel is with the government. After all, they are the people who brought into existence the very pipe lines, the very companies, that required a royal commission to look into their operations. Has the Liberal party any fundamental quarrel with what is being done now? I do not think so. The hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas), speaking for the Liberal party at the resolution stage, had this to say as found on page 3772 of Hansard.
If It is the intention of the government to follow the recommendation of the Borden commission in this respect, that is, establishing a base rate in this way, it will merely tie the hands of any board which will have to enforce the law, and at the same time it will discourage investment in Canada at a time when investment ought to be encouraged and not scared away by restrictive provisions.
The attitude of the Liberal party is, bring in more Texas buccaneers, bring in more Americans to control industries in this country and once control is obtained by them then bring in an anaemic bill which does not have the teeth in it recommended by Mr. Henry Borden, chairman, and the other members of the royal commission. The spokesman for the official opposition went on to quote Mr. Ely, the president of the investment dealers' association of Canada, in these words:
There is no doubt that the report has been a great blow to the confidence of foreign investors in Canada. Its recommendations, if implemented, will certainly impair our ability to import from abroad the large amounts of capital we require.
There is the stand of the Liberal party in opposition to the recommendations of the royal commission. In this debate, the Liberal party and Conservative party are in substantially the same position. They are prepared to see the Texas buccaneers, the pampered pets of the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, who have today become the dear dollies of the Prime Minister, continue to make out of almost zero investment-sometimes $8 and at other times no risk at all-fabulous profits ranging anywhere from one-third of a million
National Energy Board dollars up to one and a half million dollars. The people of Canada, by this legislation, are being asked to pay returns on gas and oil that will provide substantial profits to these buccaneers, not on the basis of the money they risked but on the basis of the fabulous, exorbitant and unwarranted profits that have been theirs.
The members of the Liberal party and the members of the Conservative party can smile broadly this afternoon, but what is happening under the action that has been taken is that the cost of energy required for the survival and expansion of Canadian industry, both domestic and export industries, is being increased unduly. Canada's ability to compete in the export markets is being damaged by this government. The government's attitude is, we welcome capital to make speculative profits; we are prepared to allow high prices to be charged for gas in order to pay fabulous returns on these speculative investments even though the result is high cost industry in Canada and damage to Canadian export markets.
This capitalist system, Mr. Speaker, as managed or mismanaged by the Liberals and as managed or mismanaged by this government, has shown itself not to be a free enterprise system in which the ordinary Canadian has a chance to invest and make a good return, but has shown itself to be a system which breeds, by way of clique and special privilege, millionaires and which makes multimillionaires out of existing millionaires. It is doing great damage to Canadian industry by increasing energy costs and making it more and more difficult for Canada to maintain its trade position in the world today.
I have great respect this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, for the position taken by the Conservative party in 1956. I wish I could say I had the same respect for the position that they are taking today.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
In introducing the resolution which preceded this bill on Monday last, a measure to provide for the establishment of a national energy board, and in the course of his statement in moving second reading of the bill this morning, the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) indicate that this bill offers very little new in so far as legislation is concerned. In fact, this morning the minister clearly stated that this new bill was based mainly on the principles of the Pipe Lines Act and also on the exportation of gas act. In other words, Mr. Speaker, it took a royal commission and a great deal of expense to the taxpayers of this country, plus almost two years, for the government

National Energy Board to decide to replace existing legislation which adds very little new except the name of a new board to be known as the national energy board. This board will have little additional power and limited scope, and at this early date we are not in a position to determine fully the importance of its contents after having had only a few hours to examine the bill.
The minister further stated this morning that in preparing this bill the government had in mind certain recommendations of the Borden commission. Well I intend to show, in the course of my remarks, how little attention the government has paid to the Borden commission recommendations. The minister also referred this morning to the final report of the Borden commission. I hope that before this debate is concluded the minister will tell the house when we may expect to receive the second or final report of the Borden commission. It may be that as a result of the very poor reception the preliminary report has received in the country, and the very little attention which has been given to it by the government, the final report of the commission may be some time in the future.
The minister also stated in the course of his remarks this morning that the present bill contains no provision to regulate coal, uranium and certain other sources of energy, and that the government had decided not to disrupt agencies involved in these commodities. I shall have occasion, in the course of my remarks, to deal briefly with this point. The minister stated, too, that this major issue if of very great importance to Canada's future and it should receive consideration by this house. I wonder why, if the issue is of such major importance, it was thrown at us by the government for discussion in second reading within a few hours after the bill was introduced.
In introducing this bill, the Minister of Trade and Commerce insisted that this was in fulfilment of an objective held by the Conservative party over the years. He then quoted a statement made in this house on February 25, 1955, by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, now the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) in which he expressed the need for an over-all energy policy. He quoted the minister as saying, let us get away from dealing with the problem piecemeal, with the different departments concerned. The Minister of Trade and Commerce then went on to quote the preamble of order in council P.C. 1957/1386 passed on October 15, 1957, setting up the royal commission on energy. This order in council referred to the different sources of energy in the form of gas, oil, coal, water and uranium within
[Mr. Robichaud.l
Canada's boundaries, and referred also to the increasing need of energy for the growing industrial requirements of Canada which renders it of the greatest importance to assure the most effective use of these resources in the public interest.
The royal commission appointed by this order in council was instructed, by its terms of reference, to inquire into and make recommendations in connection with certain matters referred to in detail by the minister in introducing the resolution preceding this bill. I do not intend at this stage to go into the details of the terms of reference of the commission known as the Borden commission, as the minister himself has spent some time in reviewing the content of the order in council instructing the commissioners to proceed with the study of Canada's energy problem. To my astonishment, however-and this notwithstanding the broad recommendations of the commission-I find that the study of the Borden commission to date has been rather curtailed and limited to certain aspects of the energy problems in this country quite far apart from the terms referred to in relation to the export of energy and sources of energy.
The first report made public in October, 1958 says little if anything about the use of coal for the production of energy; and even to this date, almost two years after being introduced, the commission has not yet seen fit to hold meetings in the Atlantic provinces. Is it because the coal problems of Cape Breton and Nova Scotia and of the Minto coal fields in New Brunswick are not important enough to warrant the investigation and study allotted to other sources of energy, or is it because the chairman of the said commission is so disappointed and upset by the public reaction to his preliminary report-or, I could add, to the government's reaction to his first report- that he feels reluctant to proceed further with the assignment of inquiring into and making further recommendations concerning the problems of such other related matters having to do with sources of energy not covered in this first and preliminary report.
The bill presently under discussion is nothing else but a mere repudiation by the government of the Borden commission's recommendation as contained in its first report. My colleague, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas), referred this morning to an address given at an annual dinner of the board of trade in Toronto on February 4, 1957 and quoted remarks made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on that occasion with regard to his party's policy on the setting up of a Canadian national energy board. If we look at these

remarks made by the Prime Minister, we may ask ourselves who will select the membership of the board to be appointed following the approval of the present bill? Will it be the president of the national research council or some business organizations? Would it be through the recommendation of interested provincial governments? Or will it be a board appointed to serve the best interests of the present government?
The Prime Minister has mentioned our vast resources of gas, oil, coal and uranium. Is the board to be set up for the purpose of advising and recommending proposals with regard to our resources or would it be limited to the issuing of export permits and other minor matters relating to the operations of pipe lines or other means of energy distribution? Is it only a board to replace other existing government agencies such as the board of transport commissioners under the Pipe Lines Act and those parts of the Railway Act incorporated in the same act?
In introducing his bill, the minister has referred to the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act and also to the Pipe Lines Act of 1949 which we understand will be incorporated in the present bill. Referring to the development of sources of energy, the minister has indicated that the increasing demands for electrical power have stimulated the use of most of the readily available sources of hydroelectric power. He even mentioned the fact that thermal power units based on the utilization of coal are being constructed in increasing number. The fact remains, however, that thermal power units based on the utilization of coal are becoming more and more a question mark in the development of electrical energy. It is my feeling that proposed power plants originally intended to use coal as a generating source are contemplating shifting to other sources of generating fuel.
It seems a pity that even eight months after the publication of the first report of the Borden commission-notwithstanding statements made to the contrary even in this house by the Prime Minister himself-it appears that coal has been removed from the context of studies which Canadians have every right to expect would cover all forms of energy. The problems affecting the coal mines of Nova Scotia may not be superficially connected with the studies of the Borden commission; but no one can deny that one of Canada's basic industries is left out or even singled out as if it was not of sufficient importance to the national economy to share in what was supposed to be an important and complete study on Canada's energy.
National Energy Board
Without suggesting that the existing dominion coal board should be interfered with- and I want to be clear on this point-we of the official opposition feel that the coal problem should have played a more prominent part in the study of the Borden commission. Notwithstanding statements of assurance made to the contrary by government members, we fear that our Canadian coal industry is threatened by the wide-spread expansion of natural gas and fuel oil. This is our reason for insisting that every means possible should be taken to include coal within the sphere of a royal commission set up to clarify our energy problems.
When one peruses attentively the bill presently under study and compares it with the recommendations contained in the first report of the Borden commission, he cannot help wondering why the present government had to go into the expenditure of $200,000 or $300,000 before introducing this piecemeal legislation. Here is a government whose policy has always been'

that is, if it ever had a policy at all to rely on-to maintain complete freedom and competition of trade. Today this same government is asking us to approve a measure which will regulate the importation or exportation of electric power and gas and also the importation of gas. Furthermore, this same measure will introduce a rate regulation system which sets the tolls on natural gas and this at the board's discretion subject to cabinet approval. What kind of a deal will be offered to investors when the new rates are set up? The provisions of the present bill appear to be putting the whole regulation system on a flexible basis, but no assurance whatsoever is given as to the government's attitude towards a fair treatment of investors as well as of consumers and producers.
The first report of the commission has met with severe criticism from the Canadian petroleum association. This complex document of the Borden commission, which appeared more concerned with criticism of the previous administration than with offering constructive measures which could provide greater knowledge and broader control of our energy resources, does not agree with the views of the oil and petroleum industry in Canada. In its policy statement presented to the Prime Minister on December 15, 1958 the association expressed its views in the following terms as found in the introduction on the first page of this brief:
The interim report of the Borden commission is a lengthy and complex document. Following study of this report we wish to present a reasoned and reasonable view of constructive measures that may be taken to provide Canada with greater knowledge of and broader control over its energy resources,

National Energy Board without wastefully Inhibiting development of these resources, and at the same time:
(1)	Preserve competitive free enterprise in our country;
(2)	Adhere to the principle of honouring contracts;
(3)	Maintain sound climate for investment still needed in vast amounts to turn Canada's "potential" into "reality".
The commission's report points up the complex problems created by the growing importance of oil and gas to the economy of Canada and the resulting need for adequate machinery to deal with national energy policies and regulation of interprovincial gas pipe lines. We take issue, however, with certain specific features of the commission's recommendations and offer our suggestions in the hope that the objectives of the federal government can be attained without excessive regulation of private industry or confusion and duplication between various levels and branches of government.
It is most important, Mr. Speaker, that government-imposed regulations be drafted so as not to interfere with competitive free enterprise in our country. The objective of the federal government in dealing with energy policy and regulations can be attained without interference with private industry, as suggested in this brief, and without creating confusion and duplication between various levels and branches of government. Excessive regulations and controls will result in confusion not only with investors but with producers alike. It could bar and exclude incentive and competition within the industry, thus resulting in higher costs of production passed along to consumers. The present bill might relieve somehow the apprehensions created by the publication of the first report of the Borden commission.
I have here before me the list of recommendations included in chapter 1 of the report of the commission on the export of natural gas and crude oil. How many of the said recommendations are implemented in the present bill? When we look at the first recommendation having to do with the export from Canada of natural gas which may from time to time be surplus to the reasonably foreseeable requirements of Canada permitted under licence, we find that this recommendation is included in the bill.
The second recommendation, part of which has to do with the terms and conditions of the contract under which the export is proposed to be made and the contemplated arrangements with respect to the disposal of by-products and avoidance of waste, we find is excluded from the present bill.
The third recommendation that an export permit may be granted for a period of not more than 25 years from its date is included in the bill and was referred to by the minister this morning.

The fourth recommendation that section No. 9 of regulations respecting the exportation of power and fluids and the importation of gas made and established by order in council P.C. 1955/907, in so far as it applies to natural gas, be rescinded, has not been considered by the government in preparing the present bill.
Recommendation 6, which asks that the return on the shareholders' investment in Westcoast Transmission Company Limited permitted by the board of transport commissioners shall not result in Canadian consumers of natural gas contributing more than their fair, reasonable and proportionate share of the total return, has been ignored in the present bill.
Recommendation 7, which again has to do with the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited, is not yet at least included in the present bill. The same applies to recommendation No. 9, that any application which Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited may make in the future for a licence with respect to such export be considered on its merits.
In section B having to do with crude oil, recommendation No. 10 reads:
That, having regard to the present proven reserves of crude oil in Canada and to trends in the discovery and growth of reserves, the export from Canada of crude oil be permitted under annual licence.
There is no mention of this recommendation made in the present bill.
The same will apply to recommendation No. 11, which recommends that it shall be mandatory for the board of transport commissioners for Canada to exercise the powers conferred upon it under part II of the Pipe Lines Act, etc. The same also applies to recommendation No. 12, that the prices, tolls, rates or tariffs of a company owning or operating an oil or gas pipe line, as regulated by the board of transport commissioners for Canada, should be just and reasonable, nondiscriminatory and calculated to yield a fair rate of return on the shareholders' equity, after making due allowance for reasonable and proper operating expenses, depreciation, interest, income and other taxes. Again this recommendation is completely excluded from the present bill. The same also applies to recommendation No. 13, which reads:
That legislation be enacted by the parliament of Canada to enable the government of Canada to exercise effective control over the export from and the import into Canada and the movement across provincial boundaries of all energy and sources of energy.
Recommendation No. 14 that a national energy board be established is being taken care of in the present bill. The same would apply to part of recommendation No. 15, that

the national energy board be authorized to require that anyone wishing to construct an oil or gas pipe line or one intended for the transportation of petroleum products or byproducts of the processing of gas, subject to the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, obtain a certificate of public convenience from such board. It appears that this recommendation, at least in part, replaces some of the powers of the board of transport commissioners.
Recommendation No. 16, that the national energy board be authorized to require any company engaged in the transmission across provincial boundaries by pipe line of crude oil and petroleum products and natural gas and by-products thereof to obtain a licence from such board, is included in the present bill.
Recommendation No. 17, which recommends that from time to time other forms of energy or sources of energy be brought under the authority of the national energy board for such purposes as may be specified by the governor in council, I have not been able yet to find in the present bill in the little time I have had to examine the bill. The same will apply to recommendation No. 18, which reads:
That such divisions or branches of the various departments of the government of Canada now concerned with oil and natural gas and related matters and whose responsibilities would properly come within the jurisdiction of the national energy board be transferred to its jurisdiction.
Recommendation No. 19, which has to do with the importation into Canada of crude oil and petroleum products being made subject to licence granted by the national energy board is, according to my understanding, subject to the decision of the governor in council. Recommendation 20 provides that the national energy board has certain authorities and authorizes it to give advice and make recommendations with reference to any matter relating to energy or sources of energy to any minister or to any board or agency constituted under the authority of an act of the parliament of Canada. This is partially covered in the present bill with the exception of the portion that provides that such advice be given at the request of the minister to any board or agency constituted under the authority of the legislature of any province.
Also not implemented was the portion of that recommendation which provides that the board shall compile, study and review the statistics and estimates of the quantity, quality, location and availability of the various forms of energy and sources of energy in Canada so that the board may maintain an up-to-date inventory of Canada's energy resources. Another portion of
National Energy Board that recommendation not implemented or covered in this bill is the one directing the board to co-operate with and assist any board, agency or other authority, constituted under the provisions of any act of the parliament of Canada or of the legislature of any province, having jurisdiction relating to energy and sources of energy, in establishing standards of measurements and methods of assessing and estimating supplies of energy and their sources. The balance of this recommendation concerning the granting of licences has been covered by this bill.
Recommendation 21 is covered by the bill with the exception of subsection (a) (ii) which reads:
The advisability of encouraging the development in Canada of processing industries relating to energy and sources of energy as distinct from the export of unprocessed natural resources.
It is not too clear whether this would come within the purview of Bill No. C-49.
Recommendations 22, 23, 24 and 25 which have to do with the hearings of the board are included in the bill as is recommendation 26 relating to the submission of an annual report of the board.
Recommendation 28 relating to the appointment of a member of the board to the Canadian section of the international joint commission has not been implemented nor has recommendation 29 to which reference was made this morning by the minister and which provides that if possible reciprocal arrangements be made with the United States federal power commission to have a member of that body sit as an ad hoc observer but without vote when the national energy board is considering applications for the export of national gas from Canada to the United States or for the import of natural gas into Canada.
Recommendation 30 refers to enabling legislation and is covered by this bill. Recommendation 31 relates the coming into force of the enabling legislation and has been included in the bill. Recommendation 32 is only partly covered by the bill and recommendation 33, which provides that the board of transport commissioners exercise regulatory jurisdiction as recommended by the commission in its report, has not been included. Recommendation 34 to the effect that no special measures need be taken in relation to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited in order to safeguard the interests of Canadian producers or consumers of gas has been covered by the bill.
By going through the 34 recommendations listed in the report we find that 23 have been included and 11 have been completely ignored. Out of those 32 that are listed in the present bill most represent provisions

National Energy Board already included in existing measures that are being repealed and replaced by the present legislation.
The Canadian petroleum association in its brief to the Prime Minister recommended that a national energy board could best serve the national interests if limited to fact finding and advisory responsibilities. The Borden commission also recommended that the energy board should have authority to compile, study and review the statistics and estimates of the quantity, quality, location and availability of the various forms of energy and sources of energy in Canada so that the board may maintain an up-to-date inventory of Canada's energy resources. Nowhere in the present bill do we have the implementation of such a recommendation.
Before concluding my remarks I wish to place on the record the conclusions of the Canadian petroleum association brief presented to the Prime Minister which will be found on the last page of this document. This reads as follows:
1.	That many recommendations of the Borden commission as stated in its interim report would, if implemented, result in excessive regulation damaging to the best interests of Canada.
2.	That there should be a division of energy authority as between policy making, advisory and regulatory functions.
3.	That the government should not relegate policy making to any board.
4.	That an energy board can best serve the national interest if limited to fact finding and advisory responsibilities.
5.	That regulatory powers should continue to be administered by the board of transport commissioners supplemented by the addition of an oil and gas division.
6.	That it is vital to the national interest that greater utilization of western Canada's surplus gas reserves should not be delayed and that the existing board of transport commissioners be used to expedite action at the federal level in current gas export applications.
7.	That elimination of "leverage" on pipe line shares would hinder the financing of new pipe lines in Canada, would reduce opportunity for public investment in pipe lines and would inevitably increase the cost of oil and gas to consumers.
8.	That all private business is based on sanctity of contract and no changes in government policy should be made that would fail to uphold that principle.
It is doubtful, Mr. Speaker, if the new board will meet the wishes of the industry concerned. A substantial amount of the taxpayers' money has been spent without achieving the results and accomplishments expected. Before introducing the present bill to establish the energy board the government would have been well advised to give further consideration to recommendation 18 of the commission's report which reads as follows:
That such divisions or branches of the various departments of the government of Canada now concerned with oil and natural gas and related matters and whose responsibilities would properly come

within the jurisdiction of the national energy board be transferred to its jurisdiction.
In other words our energy problems are so vital to Canada's economy that every division or branch of the various departments of the government of Canada now related to oil, gas, coal, uranium or other sources of energy, could properly come, not only within the jurisdiction of the national energy board but perhaps under the jurisdiction of a separate department of the government.
While the present bill calls for a board to consist of five members, a government whose charges of waste and extravagance were so frequent in the past could well give consideration to limiting the members of the board to three as suggested in the Borden report. In fact, the limited coverage of the present bill is an indication that the responsibilities involved could well have been taken care of by a board composed of three members instead of five as suggested in the bill.
Why has this bill, an entirely new piece of legislation, been thrown at us on 48 hours notice? We are being called upon to discuss a bill of 101 clauses, an entirely new bill, which was given first reading on Tuesday of this week and which the leader of this house was insisting that we should discuss on second reading no fewer than two days later. Now that we have been given an extra 24 hours to examine this empty piece of legislation, we are asking ourselves why such a rush on the part of the government? Now that they have waited two years before introducing this measure, why all at once this anxiety to see it through? Why, in fact, has it been introduced before the final report of the Borden commission is made public? Is it because the government is afraid to face the unpopular repercussion which has resulted from the preliminary report? Is it because the government is more anxious to legislate by cabinet decisions than by approval of parliament? We recall, Mr. Speaker, the attitude of the members of the present government when they were sitting in opposition in 1955 and were criticizing the government because the minister of defence production was asking for certain powers which he may have to use only in an emergency. We well remember the objections which were raised at that time.
My time is limited, but before resuming my seat I would suggest that this bill be sent to a special committee of the house where representatives of the industry concerned could make representations and where the bill could be given the proper study it deserves.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with regret that I have to state on rising to speak on Bill No. C-49, to provide

for the establishment of a national energy board, that I am bitterly disappointed in the bill as proposed at the present time. We in this parliamentary group have for years been expressing the need in every session for both the establishment of a national energy board and, perhaps of even more importance, a national energy policy. I can well recall when a number of the present members of the government were sitting on this side of the house to our right on those occasions, and the remarks that they had to make in support not only of a national energy board but of the establishment of a real national energy policy. Naive as I am, after all those years, I did have the thought that perhaps in this respect at least they were sincere and that when, after two years consideration in the seats of government, and after receiving the reports of a royal commission, they had reached the time of introducing a bill, it would really be a worth-while bill.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I feel bitterly disappointed. In the first place, the provisions of Bill No. C-49, although it does establish a national energy board, do not contain the authority either for a fact-finding body or the administration of a national energy policy.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the introduction of this bill, saying it is the national energy board, is a sham and a shibboleth on the members of this house and the people of this country because a national energy board should be exactly what the term implies, namely one that deals with energy in this country.
We fully realize that there are conflicts in jurisdiction. There is the jurisdiction which is strictly federal; there is the jurisdiction which is provincial; there is the jurisdiction which is interprovincial, and there is the jurisdiction which is international. Surely it should have been possible for the government to draft an act which would give full power, within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, to this board, and to have given also the board at least a consultative and advisory capacity which would try to work things out on an interprovincial as well as an international basis.
I do not think the government is trying to fool us-it cannot fool itself either-but you cannot have a national energy policy that does not take in every province and everything of an energy-producing nature in this country. If you are going to have a national energy policy you cannot consider electrical power on a provincial basis. There has to be a plan on what is known as the grid basis, as they have in the United Kingdom, a complete tie-in and control on a grid basis; that is, a tie-in of power inter-provincially and nationally. In so doing, there
National Energy Board is then the question as to whether the power should be hydro, thermal, coal or nuclear. I cannot conceive of that kind of plan being evolved except under-I will use the word "direction"-at least the consultative and advisory direction of the federal government, because power is of such an integrated nature and the developments of science are proceeding so rapidly that the best interests of the country can be served only by at least a federal body which recognizes the well-being of all Canada in so far as power is concerned, whether it be coal, thermal, nuclear, hydro, gas or oil. The fact that that principle is not recognized in this bill is, I say, a betrayal of Canada, because we are now at a time when decisions have to be made and if not definitely undertaken at least studied, and some central body should have the authority and direction to work on this most important subject.
I am most bitterly disappointed that the government has been so derelict in its understanding of the problem of the need of power that something of this nature and direction is not included in any way whatsoever in this bill. No authority whatsoever, as far as I can read the bill-and I have read it three times now-is included to enable this board when established to be able to proceed.
I am not going to speak at all, as the previous speaker did, on the Borden report itself, but I do think that note should be made as to who was the chairman of that commission. If my information is correct, and I think it is because I got it from the Financial Post directory, Mr. Borden is president of the Brazilian Traction, Light and Power Company Limited, which company I understand also has certain dealings in gas in Brazil; chairman of the Canadian board of the Norwich Union Life Insurance Company and the Norwich Union Fire Insurance Society Limited; a director of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, the Canadian Bank of Commerce, Canadian Fund Incorporated, Investment Fund Limited, International Business Machines Company Limited, National Trust Company and Massey Harris-Ferguson. He is a man who, I presume, has vast experience as a financial and industrial baron and as chairman of this royal commission he was actually investigating the operations of the financial and industrial barons of Canada.
I am going to say, because I think it is correct and therefore should be said, that with his knowledge and experience with respect to industry and finance and examining the operations of industry and finance in Canada he brought in his recommendations as a royal commissioner having in mind what

National Energy Board is in the best interests of Canada. It is rather amazing that a man of his experience and background, having examined the operations of his colleagues in Canada, should feel that in the interests of Canada certain things should be done to protect the Canadian people and yet in the vast majority of cases the government has not seen fit to follow the findings and recommendations of his report.
As I said, I am not going to speak on the actual report itself about which a great deal has already been said. What I want to do in the time I have available is to take the bill and draw what I think are very pertinent facts to the attention of the members of the house. We are discussing the principle of the bill so may I refer first of all to the explanatory note respecting the bill. I want to place particular emphasis on the explanatory note, especially the first half of it. This is what it says:
The purpose of this bill is to establish a national energy board which shall,-
I emphasize the word "shall".
-in order to assure to the people of Canada the best use of energy resources in this country, regulate in the public interest the construction and operation of oil and gas pipe lines subject to the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, the tolls charged for transmission by such pipe lines, the export and import of gas. the export of electric power and the construction of those lines over which such power is exported.
I think it is to be expected that the principle of the bill would be explained in that first explanatory note, and it definitely states that the principle is to establish a national energy board which shall assure to the people of Canada in their best interests, in the public interest, certain policies, which shall establish certain regulations and shall establish certain tolls and tariffs. Having regard to the principle of the bill I say that the explanatory note as to the principle underlying the bill is not correct in that nowhere in the bill can you find that the board to be established under this legislation shall have the power as a board to implement in the public interest what the explanatory note says is the purpose of the bill.
I think that any constitutional lawyer or lawyer skilled in interpretation will agree that the two most important words in any statute of a legislature or of the House of Commons are the words "may" and "shall". I cannot remember very many acts that have come to my attention that have had so many "mays" and "shalls". But remembering what is supposed to be the principle of the bill and the powers of the board I draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, and to that of members of the house where the word "shall" appears and where the word "may" appears. "Shall" is mandatory; "may" is permissive.

In a few sections of the bill "shall" is used a great deal. We find that there shall be a board consisting of five members. We find that the commissioners shall live in Ottawa or within 25 miles thereof. We find that the chairman, vice-chairman, and the other three members shall be paid certain remuneration. We find that the head office shall be in Ottawa. We find that there shall be a secretary appointed by the governor in council and that he shall live in Ottawa or within 25 miles thereof. There are some very definite "shalls".
When we go beyond the provisions respecting appointment of the members of the board, their salaries, where they shall live and the staff of the board and come to the powers of administration of the board it is truly remarkable how the word "shall" disappears and is replaced by the word "may". In section after section we find that, so far as policy and administrative powers are concerned, the board is not a policy making or administrative board at all. It is a political stooge of the government in power. If those hon. members who are now giving vent to sarcastic laughter have read the provisions of the bill they will know that the wording is "may", subject, almost without exception, to approval of the governor in council. I have to speak on the principle of the bill and I shall speak on the principle of "may" and "shall".
When we come to the real purpose and principle of the bill, the powers and the policies of the board, we find that on page six of the bill there is provision as to orders and decisions of the proposed board and that any decision or order of the national energy board may, for the purpose of enforcing thereof, be made a rule, order or decree of the exchequer court or of any superior court of any province. An order, decree or decision of the board is only permissive from the point of view of enforcement thereof by the exchequer court or any other court. Having made a decision, order or decree we find that under the principle of the section the board may review, rescind, change, alter or vary any order or decision. But that is subject to-the governor in council. We find, as we go through the bill that the same thing applies to almost all the regulations and administrative powers of this new, proposed board.
When it comes to what I presume is the major principle in the bill, that is the power of issuance of certificates for pipe lines and international power lines, we find that the bill does not say the board shall be able to issue a certificate for a pipe line or international power line. No, it says the board may, subject to the approval of the governor

in council, issue a certificate for a pipe line or international power line. Not only has the board not the power within itself to deal with the purposes for which we understood this bill would be introduced, but under the provisions of this bill they cannot even revoke or suspend any licence which they grant with the permission of the governor in council except with the approval of the governor in council. They cannot issue a licence without approval, and they cannot revoke or suspend a licence without approval.
I say that this principle of "may" makes the board subject at all times to the governor in council and makes it a political stooge and not a policy making or administrative board. We heard much from the minister when he spoke on this bill, and we read about the principle underlying this bill as contained in the explanatory note which I read a few minutes ago, indicating that the board shall have the power to make orders with respect to traffic, tolls and tariffs. But what does the bill say? The bill says that the board may make orders with respect to matters relating to tolls, traffic and tariffs.
If the government is sincere in the purpose for which this bill is introduced, will they kindly explain why, in connection with a major purpose which is tolls on gas and oil, the bill merely says in clause 50 that the board may do this. Why is everything subject to the governor in council and political expediency control? I do not think any of us in this group or amongst the general public expected that kind of bill to be introduced by this government. This principle goes all the way through the bill, that the board may make orders with respect to traffic, tolls and tariffs, but under governor-in-council control.
Once again I might say, as I did a few minutes ago, when it comes to the issuance of certificates for oil pipe lines, if this board wants to disallow or reconsider the issuance of a certificate it is a question of "may", not a question of "shall". This board does not have very definite administrative powers. So, we go all the way through this bill to the section dealing with the transmission of oil and the principle in this bill is that if the board has something important to do in connection with the transmission of oil, the board may, if it considers it necessary or desirable to do so in the public interest, require a company to do so and so. If the board finds, in the words of the bill, it is necessary or desirable to do something in the public interest, then why should the bill say that the board may take certain action? Surely, it should be that the board shall, in the public interest, exercise its power.
National Energy Board
As it is in connection with the transmission of oil, so is it in connection with the transmission of gas. Once again we find that if the board finds action necessary or desirable in the public interest it may take certain action. Surely, if honesty, sincerity and integrity mean anything to this government, then if it is in the public interest and if it is advisable for the board to do something the bill should provide that it shall be done, not that it may be done. All the way through, in section after section, when we come to the powers of the board under this bill there is no provision that they shall do things in the public interest; it says they may do something in the public interest. Whether or not the board may do something in the public interest is not determined by the board, but by the governor in council. I do not believe I have ever read a bill drafted in the way this one is.
If you want to go through the bill clause by clause until you come to the provision for the transmission of gas in clause 61 you will find that when it comes to the equalization of the differential between costs, if the board finds it a right thing to do, then they may take certain action. It is not that they shall, but that they may. Mr. Speaker, I say that in legal terminology the words that mean so much are "shall" and "may". The proof of the sincerity of the government moving a bill of this nature is also found in the terms "shall" and "may". A reading of this bill now before us shows that in small things like the salary of the members, how many members there can be and how long they can continue to hold office, the word "shall" is used. These are very important provisions, I realize, and the government must have given a great deal of thought to them. However, when it comes to the major provisions of the bill concerning the powers of the board itself, it is always "may" and almost without exception, subject to the governor in council.
As I said at the outset, I find myself very keenly disappointed in this bill. We had looked forward to a real bill establishing a national energy board that would have authority, that would have the powers of administration and investigation, that would have everything permissible which would enable them to do a task which is a basic requirement and an immediate necessity for Canada, that is develop a real national energy policy covering every province of our nation and all the resources which are capable of the production of energy. This bill represents a start. All I can say is it ought to be able at least to crawl if it cannot walk or run. We hope that before this bill passes, with the knowledge of modern science, the

National Energy Board knowledge of modern medicine, the knowledge of the new economists, that somehow or other the minister who introduced this bill will give it a hypodermic and bring it to life.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may be a surprise to some of the members of this house to hear me speak on gas and oil. However, I should like to inform the house at the outset that gas, particularly dry gas, is of great interest in my constituency. Throughout the past half dozen years there have been established throughout the eastern part of Alberta numbers of settlements which have sprung up primarily owing to the gas industry. In some places there is a considerable amount of oil. I therefore feel that I should perhaps say something in this debate.
I noticed that the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) asked the question, "Why spring this on us in 48 hours?" I am certain that the people in my constituency and the people in Alberta generally would not think that this government has sprung this on anybody in 48 hours. The Borden commission sat and looked into the gas industry and studied it. It was announced in the speech from the throne that an energy board would be set up. I cannot see where the hon. member gets the idea that only 48 hours' notice was given. It appears to me that he had at least four months' notice.
Then the hon. member goes on and wants to refer this matter to a committee. He refers to the recommendation in the first report of the Borden commission. I am certain a great deal of study has been given to this matter. By sending it to a committee there would just be a great deal of repetition of what has gone on before.
When the Borden royal commission was set up it was instructed to look into the policies that would best serve the national interest in relation to the export of energy and sources of energy in Canada, the problems involved, and the extent of the authority that might be best conferred on a national energy board. In brief, that was what the commission was to study. It was also pointed out that the Borden report contained 34 recommendations. Some hon. members who have already spoken have said that the Borden report was not considered. As was pointed out, 23 of the recommendations were accepted.
In setting up the Borden commission this government was not necessarily saying that it would accept every recommendation which the commission brought forward. I think they have given a great deal of study to this matter. I commend the Minister of Trade

and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) for the great amount of work he has put into this bill and the considerable amount of work that went into the drafting of it. I certainly think that the recommendations in the Borden report are evident in the drafting of this bill.
First of all, the Alberta conservation board have said they have a surplus of gas. Then the energy board will have to study the matter and see whether Canada has a surplus. In the report I think it is suggested that it has a surplus. I hope that in the near future we can export that gas. However, as was pointed out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, before any gas can be exported, the federal power commission of the United States will have to consider the question of whether they want to import gas. As the minister pointed out on May 18, a great deal of work has been done with the federal power commission in the United States in trying to bring about a flexible arrangement and one mutually satisfactory to the two parties. I sincerely believe that things will work out and that we shall export gas in the near future.
There are some who believe that the energy board, when it is set up, should control the exact profits of the industry. To anybody who believes that such a board should control the exact profits of an industry in which so much risk is involved, may I say that such a procedure might prove to be detrimental to the rest of Canada. It might have the general effect of slowing up the development of that natural resource which is the source of so much wealth and with which this country is so abundantly endowed. I would say that a great deal of consideration and study should be given to the matter before any thought was given to controlling the exact profits a company might make. Anyone who has had any experience with wells or has watched a number of wells being sunk in Alberta will know that there is a great deal of risk and a great deal of expense in connection with the drilling of wells and the finding of dry holes.
I see no objection to setting up the tolls on the gas lines. I think it is a good step. I do not think this procedure will in any way hinder the development of this industry. This government has provided for the setting up of an energy board. I think it is a good step. The board should consider the protection of Canadian interests. I am not a lawyer, but on looking over section 44 of the act, in connection with certificates of public convenience and necessity in the construction and operation of pipe lines, I find the following:
44. The board may, subject to the approval of the governor in council, issue a certificate in respect of a pipe line or an international power line if

the board is satisfied that the line is and will be required by the present and future public convenience and necessity, and, in considering an application for a certificate, the board shall take into account-
It then goes on to list five things which it shall take into account. One of them which has been evident in today's debate is found in paragraph (d) which reads as follows:
(d) the financial responsibility and financial structure of the applicant, the methods of financing the line and the extent to which Canadians will have an opportunity of participating in the financing, engineering and construction of the line;
I think this legislation sets out clearly that the interests of the Canadian people will be protected before any certificates are granted to any pipe line, and that they will certainly take a close look at the financial structure of those pipe lines. I may be wrong, but in section 47 the bill goes on to provide as follows:
47.(1) Subject to subsection (2), the board may by order, with the approval of the governor in council, revoke or suspend a certificate if, in the opinion of the board, the person to whom it was issued has violated or failed to comply with any term or condition thereof.
I think it is set out clearly that we shall have a certain amount of control over the financing, that there will be regard for Canadians and that there will be an opportunity for Canadians to participate in the financing of a given pipe line.
In the province of Alberta a surplus of gas has been declared. Right now the industry is waiting to see whether gas can be exported to the United States. As I said before, the federal power commission of the United States must first grant permission before any gas can come into the United States. As a resident of Alberta and of my own constituency I know that this could well mean a great deal more activity, a great deal more employment and a great deal more development in Alberta. I hope that in the near future we shall export gas.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the first questions which comes to the mind of any member of this house who is interested in the subject of energy is this: Why has it taken the government so long to introduce the legislation now under consideration? Those who have followed the matter recall all too vividly the words of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he spoke in Toronto on February 4, 1957. Here is what he said when speaking to the annual dinner of the Toronto board of trade:
There is a need now for the setting up of a Canadian national energy board.
National Energy Board
Then I shall skip a few words referring to the composition of the board and again quote the Prime Minister:
-to the end that the most effective use of the energy resources of Canada in the interests of the public welfare may be assured. We have vast resources of gas and oil and coal and uranium. I believe that the time has come to set up such a board whose duty it would be to advise and recommend proposals regarding these resources so that they may be safeguarded from prejudicial action now, ill-timed action to the detriment of this and future generations.
I want, Mr. Speaker, to draw attention to the Prime Minister's use of the word "now" for the setting up of a national energy board, and his further expression that the time has come to set up such a board. That was a call for immediate action. Four days after he had spoken in Toronto the Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, spoke in the House of Commons, and again expressed the view that there was a need for the setting up of a Canadian energy board. In this regard I would like to quote from Hansard for February 11, 1957, page 1159. This is what the Prime Minister had to say at that time:
In order to meet the industrial demands of Canada's future there is a need, as is set forth in the Gordon commission report, for the setting up of a Canadian energy board with a membership composed of technical personnel which might be selected by the ministers of the departments particularly interested and also by the president of the national research council. Upon that committee as well there should be representatives of industry and of the dominion and provincial governments to the end that the most effective use of the energy resources of Canada in the interests of public welfare may be assured.
So it is perfectly clear that at that time, in February, 1957 the present Prime Minister believed in and actively advocated immediate action to set up an energy board. In the circumstances it was not unreasonable, when parliament met in October, 1957, that hon. members fully expected that at the opening of parliament the speech from the throne would forecast legislation to implement the policy advocated by the Prime Minister and to establish a special board to deal with energy in all its forms. However, the speech from the throne made no mention of legislation to create such a board despite the statement of the Prime Minister in February of 1957 both in and outside the House of Commons that the time had come to set up an energy board.
But on the following day, October 15, 1957 the Prime Minister announced the setting up, not of an energy board but of a royal commission to inquire into the policies which would best serve the national interests in relation to the export of energy and sources of energy in Canada. This commission, the Borden commission as it is popularly called,

Private Bills
was also directed to make recommendations as to the extent of authority which might best be conferred on a national energy board. The terms of this commission will be found in Hansard of October 15, 1957. To say the least, Mr. Speaker, this was a strange way of making progress. The Prime Minister had advocated the immediate setting up of the board in February, 1957, but by October of that year it seemed necessary to ask the Borden commission to recommend the policies with regard to energy that would best serve the national interest and also to tell the government what powers and authority ought to be conferred upon that board.
It can justly be observed, I think, that the national energy board was put into a deep freeze, and though many observers understood that the unfreezing process would last until the election was over, not even the most cynical of these observers believed that it would take 19 months to unfreeze the board and bring it to life by formal legislation. It was not only the formation of the proposed board that was frozen over that long period. During that whole time the country, the members of this house, the public, the oil industry and investors generally, remained in complete ignorance of the policies which this government intended to follow as to the export of natural gas and energy in other forms, and indeed with respect to all forms of energy.
I have read with care what the minister said last Monday when he opened the debate on the resolution introducing the bill, and I find even yet no positive statements as to government policy on this very important aspect of the development of our natural resources. I find it even harder to understand that the minister, who spoke this morning, was not more precise in his words about the policies of the government than he was in his introductory speech when the resolution was before the house. Mr. Speaker, as we know, parliament was dissolved in February, 1958, and not unnaturally the subject of natural gas cropped up in the election.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
